newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian workers retiring younger in 1990s.
newsitem.headline: Canadian workers retiring younger in 1990s.

text.p: Canadian workers are retiring younger in the 1990s, a new study from federal agency Statistics Canada shows.
During the 1990s, the proportion of retirees under the age of 60 was double that of two decades earlier, the agency said on Wednesday.
Of all people who retired in the 1990s, 10 percent were under 55 compared with only four percent during the late 1970s, StatsCan said.
And 24 percent of all people who retired in the early 1990s were 55 to 59, compared with only 12 percent during the 1970s.
The dramatic change in retirement patterns stems partly from changes in the Canada Pension Plan, StatsCan said. In 1987, the minimum age for drawing benefits was dropped to 60 from 65.
Also, government cutbacks and corporate downsizing as well as the popularity of early retirement incentives may also have contributed to the change, the agency said.
